title: Los Angeles launches new speed cameras in the city. Here's what drivers should know
text:
Los Angeles launches new speed cameras in the city. Here's what drivers should know - ABC7 Los Angeles 
 24/7 Live Los Angeles Orange County Inland Empire Ventura County California TRAFFIC 
 New speed cameras arrive in Los Angeles. Here's what drivers should know 
 By Leo Stallworth Tuesday, October 27, 2026 1:13AM 
 Este artículo se ofrece en Español There are new eyes across L.A. trying to catch speeders. The city's first automated speed-enforcement cameras are targeting drivers going at least 11 mph over the limit. LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- Los Angeles on Monday launched a new automated speed-safety system that officials say is designed to curb speeding on some of the city's most dangerous streets.
 The program uses cameras to track speeding vehicles. Officials say speeding accounts for most crashes on city streets.
 Under the new system, cameras are triggered when drivers are traveling at least 11 mph over the posted speed limit. The cameras are designed to capture images of rear license plates and not the faces of drivers or passengers.
 The city plans to install 125 cameras by year's end, with the systems initially issuing warnings by mail during a 60-day period before fines take effect.
 After the warning period, motorists traveling 11 to 15 mph over the speed limit will face $50 fines, with penalties increasing for higher speeds. Fines could go as high as $500.
 Violations will result in civil penalties rather than traditional traffic tickets, meaning no points will be added to a driver's DMV record.
 As of Monday, cameras were operating in four areas: La Brea Avenue and First Street; Fairfax Avenue and Clinton Street; Melrose Avenue and Hayworth Avenue; and La Cienega Boulevard and Pico Boulevard.
 LaKayla Keenan, who owns a beauty salon near one of the camera locations, said she regularly sees speeding drivers and traffic collisions.
 "Hopefully, it does slow them down," Keenan said.

 While supportive of the effort, Keenan said she is uncertain whether the cameras will have an immediate impact.
 "Maybe when people start to catch on to it, they might start slowing down," she said.
 The cameras are being deployed near schools and along streets with histories of serious traffic crashes as part of a five-year pilot program intended to reduce speeding and improve roadway safety.
 City News Service contributed to this report.
